opus-5.5.text:
I think the comparison Yann makes is really about where we are in the cycle, not about the specific technology. If you go back to the early 2000s, deep learning, or neural networks, was something most of the field had basically given up on. People thought it was a dead end — kernel methods, SVMs, graphical models were the respectable thing to do. And a small group of people, Yann, Geoff Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, kept saying: no, learning representations from data end-to-end is the right way, we just haven't had the data, the compute, or the right tricks yet. Then around 2012 everything flipped very quickly.

What he's saying about world models is that we're in a somewhat similar position now. The dominant paradigm is large language models — predicting the next token in text — and it's been enormously successful, so it's natural for people to think that's the path to everything. But Yann's view, and I largely share it, is that language is a very compressed, very thin slice of how intelligence works. A child, or even a cat, builds an internal model of the physical world — how objects move, what happens if I push this, what's going to happen next — long before, or without, any language. That kind of predictive, grounded understanding of the world is what we mean by a world model, and current systems don't really have it in a robust way.

So the analogy is: today, world models feel a bit like neural nets felt twenty years ago. There's a strong conviction among some people that it's the right direction, but we don't yet have the "ImageNet moment." We don't have a clear recipe, we don't fully agree on the objective — is it pixel-level generation, is it predicting in a latent space like JEPA, how do you incorporate action and planning — and the benchmarks aren't settled. A lot of people are skeptical or think you can just get there by scaling video generation.

Where I'd add some nuance is that the timeline might be compressed compared to deep learning. Back then the field was small and compute was scarce. Now we have huge infrastructure, a lot of talent, and we've learned a lot from LLMs about scaling and data. So I don't think it will take another twenty years. But I do think it requires some genuinely new ideas, not just making the current models bigger. And honestly, that's what makes it exciting — it feels like the open, early-stage period where a researcher, even a small team, can still make a foundational contribution, much like what happened with deep learning back then.

r001.rationale: The candidate compares world models to early deep learning and describes a small group convinced it is the right direction while many others are skeptical, conveying that only a minority sees the trajectory.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses the dominance of LLMs and skepticism about world models, but does not say that people miss the emerging trajectory because their attention is occupied by other work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what Yann is really pointing at is a question of timing, and of what a field looks like right before it tips.

If you go back to deep learning around 2010 or 2011, the ideas weren't new. Backpropagation, convolutional networks, all of that had been around for decades. What was missing was the alignment of a few things: enough data, enough compute, and a handful of people stubborn enough to keep working on it when most of the community thought it was a dead end. Then ImageNet happened, and within two or three years the whole field reorganized itself around it.

World models feel similar to me right now. The core idea is also not new. Learning a model of how the environment evolves, predicting the future state, planning in that latent space, people were writing about this in the eighties and nineties. What's changed is that we suddenly have the ingredients. We have video data at scale, we have architectures that can actually absorb it, and we have a clear sense that language alone leaves something out. Current large models are extremely good at text, but they don't really have a grounded sense of physical dynamics, of what happens when you push a cup off a table. Yann's argument is that this gap is where the next big jump will come from.

Where I'd add some nuance is that the analogy tells you about the shape of the moment, not about the exact path. In 2012 there was one dominant benchmark and one dominant recipe, so progress was very legible. With world models, we don't yet agree on what the task is. Is it video prediction? Is it latent prediction, the JEPA-style view that Yann favors? Is it a model you use for planning in robotics, or a model you use to give a multimodal system better spatial understanding? Those are quite different research programs, and the field hasn't converged. So I'd say the analogy is right in spirit, that we're at a pre-ImageNet moment, but we may still be missing our ImageNet. Part of what I find exciting about working on this is that the benchmark and the evaluation question is wide open, and historically that's often been what unlocks a field.

The other thing I take from the comparison is a kind of warning. Deep learning won partly because a few groups refused to follow the consensus. If everyone in the field right now is scaling the same thing, then by definition the next breakthrough is probably not going to come from doing more of that. So when Yann makes this comparison, I read it partly as encouragement to students and young researchers: the unfashionable direction might be exactly the one worth betting on.

r001.rationale: The response compares world models to a pre-ImageNet moment and says the field has not converged, but does not say that only a small minority can see the trajectory ahead.

r002.rationale: It says most researchers are scaling the same thing, but does not attribute their failure to recognize the emerging trajectory to attention being occupied by other work.

astra-6.text:
I think he’s drawing a parallel between two research directions that ask people to commit before the results are fully convincing. With deep learning, the conviction was that learning representations would ultimately be more powerful than designing features by hand. With world models, the conviction is that intelligence needs some internal understanding of how the world works—what changes, what stays the same, and what might happen if you take an action.

But I’d separate that intuition from any particular implementation. “World model” is a broad term. Do we mean a model that predicts pixels? One that predicts abstract representations? One that can help an agent plan? Those are related, but success at one doesn’t automatically imply success at the others. Generating a plausible video, for example, doesn’t by itself establish that a model understands the consequences of an action.

So I find the comparison useful as an argument for patience and fundamental research. I wouldn’t treat it as proof that history will repeat itself. The important question is what experiments would demonstrate that these models learn something useful about the world, and that this understanding improves prediction, planning, or interaction. That’s where the conviction has to meet evidence.

r001.rationale: The candidate compares the research convictions behind world models and deep learning, but does not say that only a small minority can see world models’ trajectory.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not attribute people’s failure to recognize an emerging trajectory to being occupied with other work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Yann is pointing to a similarity in the stage of development. With deep learning, the basic idea existed long before it became the dominant approach. There were promising results, but there were also missing ingredients, and it wasn’t obvious to everyone how far the approach could go. He sees world models as being at a similar stage today: an important direction whose potential hasn’t yet been fully demonstrated.

The motivation makes sense to me. If an intelligent system is going to act in the world, it needs some ability to anticipate what will happen—how the environment changes, and how its own actions affect that environment. But that motivation doesn’t tell us exactly what the model should learn or how we should train it. Does it need to predict every detail of a future observation, or just the information that matters for a decision? That’s a fundamental question.

So I would take the comparison as a research conviction, rather than evidence that history will necessarily repeat itself. The exciting part is turning that conviction into something concrete: a learning objective, an architecture, and experiments showing that the learned model actually helps a system understand, plan, and act.

r001.rationale: The response says world models are at an early stage and their potential has not been fully demonstrated, but does not say that only a small minority recognize their trajectory.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute people’s failure to recognize the trajectory to their attention being occupied by other work.
